    American Alliance for Solar Manufacturing Trade Committee v. United States (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_25-cv-00163 / USCOURTS-cit-1_25-cv-00163-0

    FAPD-AI: In Slip Op. 26-135, dated November 2, 2026, Chief Judge Mark A. Barnett of the U.S. Court of International Trade dismissed as moot the action brought by the American Alliance for Solar Manufacturing Trade Committee, which challenged U.S. International Trade Commission final determinations that a domestic industry was threatened with, but not materially injured by, imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from Cambodia and Thailand. The opinion explains that, after the Commission's determinations, Commerce instructed U.S. Customs and Border Protection to lift the suspension of liquidation for earlier entries, and that Customs had already liquidated the entries in the relevant period. Because the court could not grant relief even if the plaintiff prevailed, it did not reach the parties' arguments on negligibility. USCOURTS-SEL-02

      FAPD-AI: On July 7, 2026, the Fourth Circuit issued an order amending its July 2, 2026 published opinion in John Doe 1 v. Office of the Director of National Intelligence, No. 25-1527. The order adds the word 'to' after 'due' on page 7 and the phrase 'so long as the reason is lawful' to the end of footnote 5 on page 9. It also changes 'right' to 'interest' on page 16, 'detailed' to 'described' on page 17, and 'Agency' to 'Agencies' on page 25. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    • Observed at 19:28:35 Eastern time ET
      John Doe 1 v. Office of the Director of National Intelligence (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-01527 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-01527-1

      FAPD-AI: In a published opinion filed July 2, 2026, and amended July 7, 2026, the Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction issued by the Eastern District of Virginia in a suit brought by nineteen career officers of the CIA and ODNI. The officers had been placed on paid administrative leave and then notified of termination following Executive Orders 14151 and 14173 and related OPM memoranda concerning diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility offices. The court held that the Agencies' Termination Regulation (AR 4-16) creates an entitlement to the reassignment consideration and internal appeal procedures it describes, with Judge Berner writing for the majority, Judge Thacker joining, and Judge Niemeyer dissenting.     Informed Consent Action Network v. FDA, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-25-05376 / USCOURTS-caDC-25-05376-0

    FAPD-AI: The D.C. Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction the appeal by the Informed Consent Action Network from a district court order that stayed, for eighteen months, proceedings on its Freedom of Information Act request to the Food and Drug Administration and required periodic status reports. The court held that the stay order is not a collateral order under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, relying on Summers v. U.S. Department of Justice because such orders are subject to revision. The disposition is unpublished and the mandate is withheld pending any timely petition for rehearing. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:10 Eastern time ET
    Carlos Galan-Sandoval v. Todd Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03999 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03999-0

    FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the Board of Immigration Appeals' dismissal of petitioner Carlos Galan-Sandoval's appeal of the denial of his application for cancellation of removal under INA § 240A(b)(1). The court held that petitioner waived any challenge to the immigration judge's hardship determination because he did not present that argument in his notice of appeal or in his brief to the Board. The court also stated that it did not need to reach the immigration judge's good moral character analysis. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:10 Eastern time ET
    Case Name in Social Security Case - Unavailable (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-05136 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-05136-0

    FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the Eastern District of Kentucky's judgment upholding the Social Security Administration Commissioner's denial of Rebecca Noe's applications for disability insurance benefits and child insurance benefits. The court found that substantial evidence supported the administrative law judge's determination that Noe's mental impairments caused only moderate limitations in the four paragraph B areas of mental functioning. The court also found that the judge adequately explained the weight given to the opinion letter of Noe's treating psychiatrist, Dr. Brian Kelty. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:09 Eastern time ET
    PPF 5 v. Delta Workover (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-60060 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-60060-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Mississippi's denial of PPF 5, L.L.C.'s Rule 60(b) motion to reinstate a case that its counsel voluntarily dismissed without prejudice under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A). The court held that the argument regarding the Mississippi Rules of Professional Conduct was raised for the first time on appeal, and that the remaining arguments were without merit or forfeited. The court noted that PPF 5 may refile its claims in any state or federal court with jurisdiction and proper venue. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:09 Eastern time ET
    NLRB v. Hotel Equities Group (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-60104 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-60104-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the National Labor Relations Board's Decision and Order and enforced the order requiring Hotel Equities Group, L.L.C., which operates a Hyatt hotel in Austin, Texas, to bargain with UNITE HERE Local 23. Hotel Equities Group had objected to the union election on the basis that union officials or employees threatened that employees who supported the union would be terminated if the union lost. The court found that the Board's factual findings were supported by substantial evidence in the record as a whole. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:08 Eastern time ET
    Chintagunta v. John Peter Smith Hosp (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-10271 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-10271-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of Anila Chintagunta's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit challenging her involuntary dismissal from medical school. The court found that Chintagunta forfeited her challenges to the dismissal of the claims against Lisa Nash, Ken Paxton, Karen Duncan, and the University of North Texas Health Science Center - Texas College of Osteopathic Medicine by not briefing the district court's grounds for dismissal. The court also held that the claim against John Peter Smith Hospital did not identify a policymaker, official policy, or custom under Monell, and denied her motion to supplement the record. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:08 Eastern time ET
    Williams v. Sanders (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-30170 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-30170-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming summary judgment for Darryl Sanders and the City of Baton Rouge on Damone Williams's excessive force claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Louisiana law. The court held that Sanders was entitled to qualified immunity because a reasonable officer could have believed Williams posed a serious threat when he reached for Sanders's loaded AR-15, including during the third shot. The court also affirmed dismissal of the related state law claims and the vicarious liability claim against the City. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the district court's denial of leave to amend and its dismissal with prejudice of David Wayne Gibson, Jr.'s pro se employment discrimination claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Louisiana Employment Discrimination Law.     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-30433 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-30433-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming a pretrial detention order entered against Lucien Augustine, who is charged with conspiracy to distribute 500 grams or more of methamphetamine. The court found the district court's factual findings not clearly erroneous, citing evidence of methamphetamine trafficking, frequent cross-country travel, and an absence from Louisiana of about 18 months after the indictment. The court also held that any error in accepting a pretrial services officer's statement without her testimony was harmless. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming a 24-month sentence imposed on Sebastian Cruz-Amaya for smuggling goods from the United States. The judgment was affirmed. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-50016 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-50016-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the dismissal of Angelica Olivas's retaliation claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act against the City of Midland. Because Olivas did not object to the magistrate judge's report and recommendation, the court reviewed for plain error and found that the district court did not plainly err in holding that she failed to exhaust the claim.     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-60491 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-60491-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit addressed consolidated appeals by Catherine and Ashley Guerdan arising from an insurance coverage dispute over tree damage to their Mississippi home. The court held that Caliber Home Loans and Pennymac Loan Services were properly served and joined, so their consent to removal was required, and that the Guerdans timely objected, which required remand of Guerdan I to state court.   • Observed at 15:43:06 Eastern time ET
    US v. Marquis Mack (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-04622 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-04622-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed the amended criminal judgment imposing an 86-month sentence on Marquis Quinzel Mack on remand, after the Supreme Court's decision in Erlinger removed the Armed Career Criminal Act enhancement. The court held that Mack's as-applied challenge to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) is foreclosed by circuit precedent and limited its Anders review to the original appeal issues and the resentencing proceedings. It found the resentencing procedurally and substantively reasonable within the advisory Guidelines range of 70 to 87 months, and found no error in the discretionary supervised release conditions. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit modified the district court's judgment to dismiss without prejudice, for lack of jurisdiction, the official-capacity claims barred by sovereign immunity, and affirmed the judgment as modified. The court affirmed summary judgment for the defendants on Nathaniel Payton's remaining Eighth Amendment claims concerning the treatment of his hyperthyroidism. The court found no genuine issue of material fact regarding substantial harm or deliberate indifference, and no constitutional violation arising from grievance handling, medical-transfer requests, or prison policies.     FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the sentence imposed on Gregorio Conde-Castillo for illegal reentry, including a 30-month above-guidelines term. The court found that the district court stated specific, individualized reasons tied to 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors, so the plain error challenge to the adequacy of reasons failed. It also rejected the preserved substantive reasonableness argument and found no reversible plain error regarding the imposition of supervised release. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:43:06 Eastern time ET
    Qashou v. City of San Antonio (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-51051 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-51051-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of Marwan Qashou's and his minor child's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit against the City of San Antonio, the San Antonio Police Department, its police chief, and two officers. The suit arose from a May 2023 arrest for driving while intoxicated, and the court held that the complaint's admission of failing a field sobriety test provided probable cause, notwithstanding a later negative blood test. The court also held that the Monell and Canton claims failed without an underlying constitutional violation, that the claims against the chief duplicated those against the City, and that the police department cannot be sued. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit vacated the district court's order denying Leon Bernard Spikes, Sr.'s fourth pro se motion for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) and remanded the case. The court found that the district court applied an outdated version of U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13 that predated the Sentencing Commission's 2023 amendment and did not explain which factors it relied on. On remand, the district court is directed to apply the current version of § 1B1.13 and provide express reasoning for its decision. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10590 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10590-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal of Darryl Payne, who was sentenced to 12 months and one day after pleading guilty to failing to register under SORNA, 18 U.S.C. § 2250(a). The court held that Payne knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to appeal in his plea agreement, that his substantive reasonableness challenge fell within the waiver, and that no exception applied. The court found that the waiver's miscarriage-of-justice exception under Hunter v. United States did not apply. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed sua sponte, for lack of appellate jurisdiction, John Michael Cohan's pro se appeal of a magistrate judge's orders denying his motion to compel a status update from a Chapter 7 trustee and his motion for reconsideration of that ruling. The court held that the orders were not final under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 because the case remained administratively stayed pending a bankruptcy proceeding, and that they were not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine. All pending motions were denied as moot. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Ellis v. US (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01814 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01814-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed, in a nonprecedential per curiam decision, the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of jurisdiction of Ernest R. Ellis's complaint concerning his 1975 Navy discharge. The court held that his medical malpractice and false imprisonment claims sound in tort, that the Due Process Clauses are not money-mandating, and that his discharge, disability retirement, and records-correction claims are barred under the six-year limitations period of 28 U.S.C. § 2501. The court also found that the Navy's alleged concealment did not suspend claim accrual. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-10734 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-10734-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed a 60-month sentence imposed on Herman Steen after he pleaded guilty to two counts of felon-in-possession of a firearm under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). Steen argued that the district court miscalculated his criminal history by assigning three points to a 2003 state drug conviction that was too old to score, while the government argued he invited the error by agreeing at sentencing that the score was correct. The court applied the invited error doctrine, concluded that Steen's later motion for reconsideration came too late, and affirmed. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 117-7, enacted April 14, 2021 and titled "An Act To prevent across-the-board direct spending cuts, and for other purposes," extends the temporary suspension of Medicare sequestration under section 3709(a) of the CARES Act from March 31, 2021 to December 31, 2021. It also amends section 251A(6)(C) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 to revise the payment reduction percentages and periods. Section 2 makes technical corrections to rural health clinic payment rules in section 1833(f)(3) of the Social Security Act and adds a continued grandfathered transition rule for certain hospitals under section 1923(g) of that Act. PLAW-SEL-01

    Public Law 117–9: To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act with respect to the scope of new chemical exclusivi… (opens in a new tab)
    Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-117publ9

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 117-9, approved April 23, 2021 and titled "An Act To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act with respect to the scope of new chemical exclusivity," replaces the phrase "active ingredient (including any ester or salt of the active ingredient)" with "active moiety" as defined in 21 CFR 314.3 in multiple provisions of Chapter V, including sections 505, 512, 524, 529, and 565A. It also revises the advisory committee referral requirements in section 505(s), the approval deadline provisions in section 505(l)(2)(A), and related rare pediatric disease and biological product provisions. Technical corrections repeal certain clauses in sections 505(c)(3)(E) and 505(j)(5)(F) and update a cross-reference in section 505A(c)(1)(A)(i)(II). PLAW-SEL-01

    Update and Clarification of the Passenger Facility Charge Regulations (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-04 / 2026-22450

    official summary: On September 27, 2023 FAA published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend its Passenger Facility Charge (PFC) regulations to implement congressionally mandated changes to an existing pilot program within the PFC program. FAA also proposed to reaffirm existing program requirements and update or remove obsolete references within the PFC regulations. Following publication of the NPRM and before FAA issued a final rule, the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (the 2024 Act) was signed into law on May 16, 2024. Several sections of the 2024 Act necessitate changes to PFC regulations or modifications to proposals made in the NPRM. As such, FAA now issues this supplemental proposal addressing: PFC turnback reductions; two new PFC-eligible projects; restrictions to PFC-eligible projects; FAA's timeline for review and acknowledgement of notice of intent (NOI) submissions; PFC streamlining review eligibility; and PFC submittal requirements. This proposal aligns with the requirements established by the 2024 Act. FR-SEL-02

    Airworthiness Directives; Pilatus Aircraft Ltd (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-04 / 2026-22496

    official summary: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2025-20-02, which applies to all Pilatus Aircraft Ltd. (Pilatus) Model PC-24 airplanes. AD 2025-20-02 requires incorporating a temporary revision into the existing airplane flight manual (AFM) for the affected airplanes, which revises the Abnormal Procedures Section. That action was considered an interim action. Since the FAA issued AD 2025-20-02, updated software has been developed and instructions have been issued for installing the software. In addition, revised operational instructions have been issued that are applicable after installation of the updated software. This proposed AD would require installing the updated software and incorporating the applicable revised operational instructions into the AFM. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-02

    Statutory Lien (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · NATIONAL CREDIT UNION ADMINISTRATION · FR-2026-11-04 / 2026-22536

    official summary: On February 25, 2026, NCUA (or `agency') published a proposed rule to solicit comments on the removal of a provision of NCUA regulations regarding federal credit unions' (FCUs) statutory lien authority. Upon further consideration, and based on the comments received, the Board is issuing this final rule, as proposed, to remove the term, “except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law.” This language does not provide any assistance to FCUs in determining whether such statutory or case law exists, therefore it has no material value. FR-SEL-01

    official summary: The NCUA Board (Board) is amending its regulations governing member business loans and commercial lending. This action is necessary to reduce regulatory complexity and improve the clarity of the NCUA's regulations.
